explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. They were sent to catch Jesus in His words (Mark 12:13). Pharisees, strict keepers of the law, and Herodians, who backed Herod's family, showed up with a question that was really a trap. It's like a coworker saying "quick question" when it's NOT quick and it's NOT a question.

explanations.answer: Ask Jesus to heal their sick
explanations.explanation: No get-well cards in these hands, friend. The text says the leaders sent the Pharisees and Herodians to catch Jesus in His words. Pharisees were strict keepers of the law, and Herodians backed Herod's family. Nobody in this visit is carrying a sick person, just a plan.

I see why you went there, since the Herodians back Herod's family. But the text says they were sent to catch Jesus in His words. Nobody's whispering a warning here. I think a visitor with a plan and a smile is a lot different from a friend with a heads-up.

explanations.answer: Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. They asked, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" (Mark 12:14). Caesar was the Roman emperor, so it's a loaded question about money and power. All that sweet talk was just the butter before the hammer.

explanations.answer: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: That one's a real question the Pharisees cared about, but it's not this one. In Mark 3:2 they watch Jesus to see whether He'll heal on the Sabbath. Here they ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" (Mark 12:14). Different day, different trap.

explanations.answer: Is it lawful for a man to divorce
explanations.explanation: Close in style, since the Pharisees did ask Jesus about divorce in Mark 10:2. But that's a different day. In this passage the question is, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" (Mark 12:14). Same "is it lawful" opening, whole different topic.

Jesus did NOT fall for the flattery, friend. The text says He "saw through their hypocrisy" (Mark 12:15). They called Him honest, but their words weren't honest at all. He asked them, "Why are you testing Me?" and the compliments went flat.

Right, He didn't buy it. Mark 12:15 says Jesus "saw through their hypocrisy" and asked, "Why are you testing Me?" They laid on the compliments, but He saw what was under them. I've had folks butter me up before, and I always check my pockets.

explanations.answer: Whose image and inscription are on it
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He asked, "Whose image is this? And whose inscription?" (Mark 12:16). He doesn't need a lecture, just a coin and two simple questions. Sometimes the best answer is already sitting in your pocket.

explanations.answer: How much the coin is really worth
explanations.explanation: Nobody's checking the price here. Jesus asked about the face and the writing on the coin. The text says, "Whose image is this? And whose inscription?" (Mark 12:16). The value never comes up.

explanations.answer: Who gave them the coin to bring
explanations.explanation: The text never has Jesus ask where the coin came from. They simply brought it, and He asked, "Whose image is this? And whose inscription?" (Mark 12:16). It's the coin itself He wants them to look at. I think He wanted them to read the answer off the coin.
Yep, "Caesar's," they answered (Mark 12:16). Even the men setting the trap had to say it out loud. Their own answer set up what Jesus said next.

I get it, since Herodians were in the group. But when Jesus asked whose image and inscription were on the coin, they answered, "Caesar's" (Mark 12:16). Herod's name doesn't come up on that coin. Good guess for a Herodian, though.

Pilate shows up later in Mark (Mark 15:1), but not on this coin. When Jesus asked whose image and inscription were on it, they answered, "Caesar's" (Mark 12:16). Caesar, the Roman emperor, was on the coin. Keep Pilate in your pocket for another day.

explanations.answer: Give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's
explanations.explanation: That's what He said, baker: "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (Mark 12:17). No yes, no no, just one answer that handled both. The coin had Caesar's image on it, and that was the point of His question. I've never seen a trap close so quietly.

explanations.answer: Give Caesar nothing and give it all to God
explanations.explanation: That's not what Jesus says. He says, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (Mark 12:17). Caesar is named right there in His answer. He doesn't tell them to give Caesar nothing.

explanations.answer: Pay Caesar first and give God what is left
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but there's no leftovers plan in the text. Jesus says, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (Mark 12:17). He names both, and neither one is the afterthought. God's part isn't a tip jar.
They did, friend. Mark 12:17 says they "marveled at Him." These guys came to catch Jesus and left with their mouths hanging open. I know that feeling, since I once tried to out-talk a rubber band.
They did marvel. Mark 12:17 says, "And they marveled at Him." They showed up with a trap and a stack of compliments, and left amazed at His answer. That's quite a change from "gotcha."

Right on, baker. "Then the second one married the widow, but he also died and left no children" (Mark 12:21). That fits the rule Moses wrote, which said a brother was to marry his brother's widow (Mark 12:19). The Sadducees are building their story one brother at a time.

Nobody packs a bag in this story. The text says, "Then the second one married the widow" (Mark 12:21). The Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, were following the rule from Moses, Israel's leader, in Mark 12:19. This brother steps up, not out.

A priest never shows up in the Sadducees' story. The text says, "Then the second one married the widow" (Mark 12:21). That matches the rule from Moses, Israel's leader, that a brother marry the widow (Mark 12:19). It's a story with seven brothers and zero detours.
Yes, that's how they tell it. "In this way, none of the seven left any children" (Mark 12:22). That's the whole setup for their big question. Seven brothers and not one little footprint in the flour.
The Sadducees say the opposite. Mark 12:22 has them saying, "none of the seven left any children." That's the setup for their question. If even one had a child, there'd be no puzzle to ask.

explanations.answer: Whose wife will she be in the resurrection
explanations.explanation: That's the question, baker: "In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her" (Mark 12:23). The Sadducees don't believe in the resurrection, so I think they were hoping the puzzle would knock it over. Seven husbands is a lot of names on one box.

explanations.answer: Which of the brothers she loved the most
explanations.explanation: Love never comes up in their question. They ask, "In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be?" (Mark 12:23). They're asking about the resurrection, not about favorites. The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, so that's the thing they're poking at.

explanations.answer: Where her seven husbands should be buried
explanations.explanation: No gravesite talk here, friend. The Sadducees ask, "In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her" (Mark 12:23). Their whole question is about the resurrection. The brothers' burial plans never come up.

explanations.answer: The Scriptures or the power of God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Aren't you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God?" (Mark 12:24). Two things, and they're missing both. That's a lot of missing for one question.

explanations.answer: The temple or the ways of the priests
explanations.explanation: Not those two. Jesus says they're mistaken because they "do not know the Scriptures or the power of God" (Mark 12:24). He's pointing at God's Word and God's power, not at temple business.

explanations.answer: The feasts or the laws of the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Those don't come up here. Jesus says, "Aren't you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God?" (Mark 12:24). The two things are the Scriptures and the power of God.
Jesus says the opposite, friend. "When the dead rise, they will neither marry nor be given in marriage" (Mark 12:25). That clears up the seven husbands puzzle. No wedding, no problem.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "When the dead rise, they will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven" (Mark 12:25). So the Sadducees' question about whose wife she'd be doesn't work the way they thought. Even I'd have to put down the wedding cake pan, and I don't even own one.

That's the one. Jesus asks, "have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses" (Mark 12:26). That's where God spoke to Moses, and the line Jesus quotes comes from Exodus 3:6. A bush on fire and still the Sadducees missed the point.

explanations.answer: The crossing of the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: Great scene, but Jesus doesn't point there. He says, "have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses" (Mark 12:26). The bush is where God said, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob."

That's not the scene Jesus names. He points them to the burning bush in the Book of Moses (Mark 12:26). That's where God told Moses, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Good thing the bush wasn't hard to spot.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living" (Mark 12:27). God said "I am the God of Abraham" long after Abraham died, so Abraham must still be alive to Him. That's Jesus making the case with one verse from the Book of Moses.

A sweet word, but it's not the one Jesus uses. He says, "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living" (Mark 12:27). The word is "living," and it's the heart of His point about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

I see where you're going, but that's not the word. Jesus says, "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living" (Mark 12:27). The word is "living." That's how He answers the Sadducees about the resurrection.

explanations.answer: Which commandment is the most important
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The scribe asks, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" (Mark 12:28). A scribe is a teacher of the law, so this is his home turf. He wanted the top one, no tie allowed.

explanations.answer: What must I do to inherit eternal life
explanations.explanation: That question is real, but it's asked by someone else. In Mark 10:17 a man runs up and asks Jesus, "what must I do to inherit eternal life?" Here the scribe asks, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" (Mark 12:28).

explanations.answer: Who then can be saved by God
explanations.explanation: That's a different day and a different group. In Mark 10:26 the disciples ask, "Then who can be saved?" The scribe here asks, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" (Mark 12:28).

explanations.answer: Love the Lord your God with everything
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength" (Mark 12:30). First comes who God is, then comes loving Him. And He says it's the most important of all.

explanations.answer: Keep the Sabbath and make it holy
explanations.explanation: That's a commandment, but it's not the one Jesus gives here. He says, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength" (Mark 12:30). That's the most important one, in His words (Mark 12:29).

explanations.answer: Bring your offerings to the temple
explanations.explanation: Not this time. Jesus answers, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength" (Mark 12:30). Offerings come up later, when the scribe says loving God and neighbor is more important than burnt offerings and sacrifices (Mark 12:33).
Jesus says no such thing, friend. He says, "No other commandment is greater than these" (Mark 12:31). The two He names sit at the top, side by side.

That's right. Jesus says, "No other commandment is greater than these" (Mark 12:31). He gave the scribe two: love the Lord your God, and love your neighbor as yourself. Nothing bigger is hiding in the back of the cupboard.

That's what he says, baker. The scribe says loving God and loving your neighbor "is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices" (Mark 12:33). Burnt offerings were sacrifices of the law, and he ranks love above them. That's a big thing to say out loud.

explanations.answer: All the scrolls of the prophets
explanations.explanation: The scribe never says that. He says loving God and loving your neighbor "is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices" (Mark 12:33). Scrolls aren't on his list.

explanations.answer: All the gold in the temple
explanations.explanation: Gold doesn't come up here. The scribe says loving God and loving your neighbor "is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices" (Mark 12:33). That's the comparison he makes.

Yes, baker. "When Jesus saw that the man had answered wisely..." (Mark 12:34). This scribe came with a question, listened to the answer, and repeated it back. That's how you win a good word from Jesus.

Nope, not even close. Mark 12:34 says Jesus saw the man "had answered wisely." The scribe said back what Jesus taught him, and Jesus noticed. I've given plenty of foolish answers in my day, but this wasn't one.

That's not how Jesus sees it. The text says He saw the man "had answered wisely" (Mark 12:34). The scribe agreed with what Jesus said about God and neighbor. Jesus even tells him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God."
He did. Jesus says, "You are not far from the kingdom of God" (Mark 12:34). That's Jesus speaking to the scribe who answered wisely. After the other questioners, that's a warm word to hear.

Jesus actually says it. After the scribe answered wisely, He tells him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God" (Mark 12:34). That's Jesus' own word to the man. Not a bad day at the office for a scribe.
